utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning technicians and interpreters. Are you ready? Very well, let's begin with the case before us today. On that note, would Mr. Mark Dubuisson please inform us of which matter is before us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is case IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mark Dubuisson. For the Prosecution we have the same as yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, I appear with my colleagues Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. And for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, learned colleagues from the Prosecution. My name is Goran Mikulicic and together with my colleague, Mr. Joka, we are representing the accused in this case, Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let us then continue, Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would like to call witness Kata Vidovic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Do you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now read the solemn declaration which the court usher will be handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the moment, you shall be responding to the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, who is there. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am an attorney representing Zlatko Aleksovski in this case. My name is Goran Mikulicic, I will ask you several questions and I would kindly ask you to answer them to the best of your knowledge and recollections. For the record, Mrs. Vidovic, when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I was born in Busovaca on the 15th of October, 1958.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a religious person?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I am Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, have you always lived in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Town of Busovaca itself or?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I was born in Kacuni and raised there and after I got married I moved to the Town of Busovaca, but this is all within the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I completed secondary medical school in Sarajevo in 1977.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What stream did you complete?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: General stream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find a job immediately after finishing school?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: It was on the 27th of September, 1977.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you find a job?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: At the Busovaca Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: At the same health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've been working at the health centre in Busovaca from 1977 until today, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What jobs did you have at the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I worked for the epidemiological department until the war. And after the break-out of the war, I started working as a nurse at the x-ray department and again at the epidemiological department as an x-ray technician and I also worked for the emergency unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in the first half of 1993, you were employed as an x-ray technician, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mrs. Vidovic, at that time, I am referring to the first half of 1993, after the break-out of the conflict on the territory of the Busovaca municipality, do you remember the structure, the organisation of work at the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: It was organised through the emergency unit. We were all employed at the emergency unit because of the increased number of cases at the emergency unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, because of the events that were taking place in Busovaca at the time, because of state of war, we had to have larger shifts and we had to be prepared because of the emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had duty service?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was a shift?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: A shift would last 24 hours, which was followed by 48 hours off duty and then again we would take a 24 hour shift and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the medical services were tendered at the Busovaca Health Centre round the clock?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, round the clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, who were the physicians who were on your shift?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Most of the time it was Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, when was the first time that you encountered patients who were brought to the Busovaca Health Centre from the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: It was in late January, early February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember these patients because there were something extraordinary about them?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, there were no differences for us among patients, they were all the same for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you about your impressions about patients coming from Kaonik. What was their general physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, their general physical appearance did not differ from the outward appearance of other patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any cases of malnutrition, untidiness, any particular injuries?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I did not notice any such case while I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were on duty, since you were also working as an x-ray technician, did you ever have an opportunity to make an x-ray examination of any of the patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I never had such a case on my shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe, and I am referring to the Kaonik patients, did you observe any symptoms of skin diseases on those patients? Were they infected with any diseases?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I did not notice any such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, do you remember who it was who brought these patients to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: They were brought by Mr. Aleksovski in person and other guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you remember how they were brought to the health centre, did they come on foot?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, they never came on foot. As for the specific vehicle, I couldn't tell you more about that, but, in any case, they didn't come on foot of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these individuals were in any way restrained or handcuffed when coming to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, they didn't, their hands were never tied up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about the procedure that was applied when they would come to have medical examination at your centre?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: We would be usually informed by the guard that a patient had been brought there. And then depending on the amount of work that we had at the time, we would admit them right away. If not, they would have to wait. I mean, the treatment was the same as with all other patients. It all depended, as I said, on the amount of work we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, do you remember whether those patients had the opportunity to express themselves directly to the doctor in connection with their complaints?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they would be alone with the physician and they would describe their problems to the physician and then the physician would prescribe adequate therapy and this was followed or applied by us, paramedics, and they would be returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, what was the usual therapy that was prescribed by the physician in view of their complaints?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: In most of the cases, they suffered from some chronic diseases, the diseases that they had from before. Usually it was a high blood pressure, a stomach pain, some chronic problems, back pain, and similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what therapy was usually prescribed by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Sometimes it was oral therapy or parenteral therapy, that is either tablets or injections, depending on the particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, was there ever a case where additional check ups were necessary?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases and these people would come back for check ups if it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, did you or any of your colleagues ever refuse to examine such patients?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, this is not allowed in accordance with our medical ethics and such thing never happened while I was on duty at the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, did you personally, because you lived in Busovaca, know any of the patients from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I knew some of them. Some of them I didn't know. I didn't know everyone in Busovaca, but I knew superficially a number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have personal contact with these people?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, most often we wouldn't have time for that because of the amount of work we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that the work had increased at that time?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many patients did you treat per day?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, it depended. It varied between 50 or 60 because they were all processed through the emergency unit. The only department that functioned separately at the time was the dentist office. The rest was all emergency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mrs. Vidovic, that the health centre in Busovaca was the only medical institution on the territory of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the entire population of Busovaca received medical health at the centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, whatever was necessary to conduct in medical health protection terms at that time was done at the medical centre in Busovaca, including the emergency service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, are you aware of the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I have never been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any of your colleagues, physicians, from the health centre ever went to that facility?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, a colleague of mine went for an intervention there and then on two occasions, we conducted fumigation and that was all. A colleague of mine went there to give an injection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the circumstances of that particular case when your colleague went to Kaonik for an intervention, was that upon an invitation or did she go there on her own?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, when a patient was examined, we would apply adequate therapy and we would perform whatever was prescribed. In this particular case, it was necessary to give an injection to the patient and that's the reason why she went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, Mrs. Vidovic, you mentioned that you also worked for the epidemiological service, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of that assignment that you had, are you aware that at the time in the territory of the Busovaca municipality, are you aware of any infectious diseases, any epidemiological problems that required intervention of your service?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any such problems because we reacted on time and we carried out fumigation at all facilities that required so, such as the Kaonik facility and the local kitchen where the food was prepared and so on. So we did not have any infectious disease at the time in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned some preventative action conducted by the epidemiological service?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned the prison at Kaonik, the Draga barracks, the health centre itself, were there any other such facilities that required such type of intervention?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: I went to the morgue to conduct fumigation on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, in addition to the patients from Kaonik, there were other patients at the health centre at the time?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We had a gynaecological service, children were examined at the centre, whoever needed medical help would come to the medical centre because that was the only medical institution in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the circumstances and because of the war at that time, did you provide medical help to HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, HVO soldiers, civilians, everyone passed through the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any separation? Did you treat separately patients from Kaonik as opposed to all other patients?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, as I said, this is something that is not allowed by our ethics and we treat all patients the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am afraid you don't understand my question, I will rephrase it. At the health centre, was there a separate space, separate room where you provided medical help to the patients from Kaonik or whether all medical services were provided at the same premises?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: They were all provided at the same premises. All patients would wait in the same waiting room in the corridor and they would all be admitted to the same surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mrs. Vidovic, that sometimes you would have in the same corridor, patients from Kaonik and HVO soldiers who were wounded and who needed medical help?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, we had cases like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any incidents in that regard at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, you stated that HVO soldiers were also given medical help at the centre, how was it that you knew that they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: They would come to the centre and they had an HVO patch, Croatian Defence Council insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw HVO insignia on their uniform, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that insignia, HVO insignia, did you ever see any other type of insignia on soldiers' uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, do you remember if the guards who would bring in patients from Kaonik or Mr. Aleksovski, do you remember if they had any insignia on their uniforms, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KATA VIDOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would conclude the examination-in-chief. We have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. For the Prosecution, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No questions in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I suppose you don't have any cross-examination, or rather, re-examination. Madam, Vidovic, you've just completed your testimony here before this International Tribunal. We thank you very much for coming and we wish you a pleasant trip back to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the next witness is brought in, Mr. Mikulicic has kindly provided me a brief summary of what this witness will testify about and has also showed me some materials, so I have some notion of what the testimony will be about. In another case, a similar witness was called, a judge, to testify and I objected to the judge testifying about cases that he was himself directly in. I based that objection on the fact that, in my submission, it's inappropriate for judges to come before this Tribunal and to give testimony about matters which they, themselves, handle as judges in Yugoslavia. It's my position that the reception of this sort of evidence is inappropriate. There's a dilemma, which I can see in this particular case because there's an aspect I feel, or apprehend, that Mr. Mikulicic would argue that while it was necessary for him to demonstrate when there were, in fact, breaches of the conventions, some actions were taken and that he needs to call this type of evidence to demonstrate that matters were not permitted to simply go unpunished or undealt with. So it does -- and, of course, that's properly admissible evidence -- so it does create a dilemma. In the other case I was involved in, there was no element or aspect of this in it, so my objection was more soundly based, if I can put it that way. I still think that the principle of judges appearing before Your Honours and testifying about cases they are involved in is inappropriate. But I can see that there is some need to overcome this issue of demonstrating that action is taken against people who breach the Geneva Conventions during the course of the conflict. There is some documentary material that Mr. Mikulicic has provided me with. It seems to me that there can be no objection to that being tendered to Your Honours to demonstrate this point. It seems to me that a witness could appear before you and say that he was, in fact, a judge and that he did deal with a certain case and so long as he didn't discuss the merits of the case, or any opinions he had, or any conclusions or findings he made, I don't believe that ought to be objectionable. I raise the matter now in the absence of the witness because I don't want to embarrass the witness, but I think that it is a matter that does need to be explored before the witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. I think this is a relevant issue. I would like to have the opinion of Mr. Mikulicic on this issue. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence understands the dilemma which the Prosecution faces, and the Defence also has its views on it. So may I be allowed to explain them. To begin with, the Defence holds that the fact that a potential witness was a judge should not mean that such a witness would be inadmissible. We do not intend to adduce evidence by questioning this witness by asking him questions regarding his conclusions, his decisions, in a particular case. By questioning this witness, Mr. Percinlic, the Defence wishes to demonstrate before this Court that even in wartime certain judicial functions were performed. By calling this witness, the Defence wishes to demonstrate the structure of the judiciary which functioned one way or the other in that area, and, needless to say, the Defence wishes also to show that measures were taken against perpetrators of individual acts, excessive acts, which could be attached, which could be ascribed to the Kaonik facility. And that is all. The Defence will try to confine itself to that aspect of activity and will not go into the acts of that particular witness in a particular court case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see that the opinion expressed by Mr. Mikulicic is not far from the opinion you've expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think if that constraint is exercised by the Defence, then the judge is not asked to express opinions on accused persons and what he thought of them and things of that nature, I don't see how that could be offensive. I think that there is a legitimate issue here for the Defence to explore, and that's why I saw it as a dilemma. But if the Defence are constrained in their questioning of this witness, I can't see how that would be offensive. I raised the objection because in the other case I objected, and my objection was sustained, and the Court did consider it inappropriate to hear evidence from a judicial officer about a particular case. So that's why I raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: One moment while I consult with my colleagues. I believe we are all in agreement that the subject of this testimony will not go to the substance of any conclusions, but rather merely touch upon the issues that we have already talked about before this Chamber. So the Chamber deems that this testimony is admissible. I think we should be concerned about not going beyond the limits of this objection, because, as Mr. Niemann stated, we do not want to embarrass the witness. And so if you will respect this principle, then I think this will be in the interests of justice and in the interests of arriving at the truth that this witness appear. With that said, Mr. Mikulicic, we may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence calls Mr. Zelko Percinlic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are now going to read the solemn declaration, which the Court usher has before you. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you are going to respond to questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Percinlic. My name is Mr. Mikulicic, and I am representing the accused, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, together with Mr. Joka in this case. We shall now ask you some questions and shall ask you kindly to answer them to the best of your recollection. I should also like to ask you to take care, to be slow enough so that the interpreters can keep up with you, so that they know what the two of us are talking about. Mr. Percinlic, will you please state for the record when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 26th of January, 1960, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a believer, a religious person?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your religion?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what your education is?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of law in 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the completion of your studies, what did you do? Did you get a job or did you do something else?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I was in the judiciary, that is, I was with municipal courts as an associate and a judge. So I was with the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, having graduated, you then began to work in the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I am at present in the district, in the regional court. So in the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which region is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Number 6 or canton number 6, Central Bosnian region, with a seat in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are the minister of the judiciary there?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the regional government?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Since when were you occupying this post?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Since May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do before May, 1996?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Before that I was the judge in the high court in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what duty did you discharge in early 1993, that is during the conflict in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I was the presiding judge of the district military court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, could you tell us how was the judiciary organised in the Territorial Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It was twofold, one could say. There were military courts and HVO courts. Those were two components of the armed forces which existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. So there were the district military court, and such only existed in Travnik and had a seat in Travnik. There were five judges and the presiding judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when the district military court in Travnik was established?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It was established towards the end of 1992, on the eve of Christmas of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the court what was the jurisdiction of that court?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The local and the real -- the Central Bosnia was under its jurisdiction. It would be some eight to, I think, ten municipalities. And, as far as other competencies, it covered the crimes against the armoured forces, all conventional crime, if the perpetrators were the members of the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which was the court of appeal, which was higher instance?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The higher instance was the civilian court. The civilian court, the higher court also with a seat in Travnik for some crimes or, rather, department of the Supreme Court in Sarajevo with a seat in Mostar, also for certain crimes, that is, the crimes tried by a chamber of judges. And the military court in Travnik, they were tried by individual judges. That is, they did not have a chamber of judges, just one judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Percinlic, that those military courts, which were established towards the end of '92, were under the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the higher instance in the civilian judiciary?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the appeals against the rulings of military courts were ruled by civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Percinlic, why were the military courts set up at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: They were set up for two, I should say, principle reasons. The first reason was that in any state of war the crime rate usually is on the rise. And a second reason is that in 90 percent of the cases the perpetrators were military, that is members of the HVO or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the court in Travnik, where you were the presiding judge, was the Municipality of Busovaca jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, will you tell us where did -- how were the judges, I mean the military judges in the military court, were elected?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: They came from the -- the basic court in Travnik and in part from the basic court in Zenica, that is former civilian judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So military judges -- so the role of military judges was performed by judges who were professional judges?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they professional -- were they professional soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, they were all civilians. They were all judges by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, one can assume that a court which conducts individual proceedings on the basis of certain criminal charges also needs to order detention; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where was the detention unit at the time, where suspects were placed before the proceedings in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, that is when the court was established, and under the legal provisions we also set up a detention unit at the ministry in Mostar. It was decided that the seat of that detention unit should be in Busovaca. Those were the early days of the organisation of that unit in Busovaca, and it was sometime towards the end of 1992 and in the early 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the facility where the detention unit was accommodated?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In view of the then possibilities, it was then put in the barracks or in the depot in Kaonik. As far as I know, it was a former JNA barracks, although before that I never even knew of the place because I lived elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And does that mean, Mr. Percinlic, that that detention unit, which was organised in the former JNA barracks towards the end of '92, was not a unit built for the purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I can assume, and I stand corrected -- you can correct me if you like, does this mean that some construction or reconstruction works had to be conducted in order to suit it for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I know that some reconstruction was needed, but I took no part in that, since it was not under my jurisdiction. It was only the detention of these people. But, yes, I could see that some construction works were underway, were completed, so that that particular facility could be turned into cells, whatever you call it, a detention facility place where detained persons could be kept under custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had only a supervisory function. What does it mean, supervisory function over the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, supervision over the detention unit, by the criminal proceedings law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, meant -- that is after Bosnia-Herzegovina separated from Yugoslavia, you may put it that way, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a decree and took over the Criminal Proceedings Act, which was formally also the Federal Criminal Proceedings Act and as such was also in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of its provisions said that a presiding judge also conducted supervision over detainees while they were kept under detention. What it meant is that their stay there, their treatment, hygiene, and all the other conditions in detention for the duration of their detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I assume that you also personally went to see that particular facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Percinlic, when was the first time that you visited the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I visited it for the first time on the eve of the new year of 1992, in order to see who was in that detention unit, who was kept under custody, because meanwhile the basic courts, rather the municipal courts, turned over their cases to the newly established military courts. And it, therefore, was necessary to see who was under custody, what they were charged with. And we also supervised the maintenance of that particular facility. That was the first time I saw the premises of the former barracks, and then I saw that some construction works had been performed. As a matter of fact, at that time they were not yet even completed. They were underway. They were in their early stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, Mr. Percinlic, by coming there as the newly appointed presiding judge of the military court in Travnik, you already found some detainees there in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you visit Kaonik frequently?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: You mean in '92 or in '93?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In '93, later.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In '93 I only came only once, that is until sometime until mid-January 1993, when the well-known events took place, and when communications were cut off between Travnik and that place -- rather, between the military court in Travnik and the detention unit in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long were the communications cut off? Did it last throughout the first half of '93 or were there intervals where the communication was re-established?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It lasted without interruption for at least a month or two, even though there was a certain communication, that is the telephone, the faxes, one could send a fax and receive a fax, or by some military communications. But there was no physical contact. That is, one could not go there. At least I could not go there because it was not safe to travel from Travnik to the site of the prison in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the first half of January, '93, you visited Kaonik once. And when was the next time that you went? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I went there next towards the end of March, 1993, in the latter half or the end of March, I can't remember exactly. But it must have been the end of March '93 or after the 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume that you came to perform supervision or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only for the supervision, because there was no supervision for almost two months, for these objective reasons that I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of people did you find in the district military prison in Kaonik? What was their structure, I mean insofar as the proceedings were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, there were detainees. Ninety-nine percent of them were detainees. And that is people charged for things that are new from the cases that had been filed with our court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these individuals, that is the detainees and those cases in the courts, did you find any other individuals there?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, do you know, within that area where Kaonik Prison is, how many buildings are there? Did you ever visit them?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. There were several buildings. At the entrance there is a building, I don't know what its purpose is, then this place where the detention unit was. From the outside you see that it must have been a hangar or something like that. And behind that building, some hundred metres behind, there was another hangar. And other facilities, other parts of that, I don't know what they were, because it's a very large complex and I never visited them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the buildings that you went into?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only the first building. That is where the detention unit was. I never entered any other building there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, will you tell us, do you know Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I met him towards the end of March, 1993. That is, I met him personally then. Otherwise, we spoke on the telephone for the first time sometime towards the end of February or in the beginning of March, '93. I can't remember exactly, because so long ago, but that was roughly about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you saw him today?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see him among the persons in this court?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He is behind your back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness stated that he could recognise the accused behind the Defence, and indicated with his hand in this direction. Mr. Percinlic, you said that before you met Mr. Aleksovski in person that you spoke to him on the telephone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity did you communicate with him?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: As the presiding judge of the district military court, and he was the warden, the commander of the district military prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you -- how did you learn or from whom did you learn that Mr. Aleksovski was the commander, the warden of the district military prison?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was also sometime in the early January, 1993. I was informed by a civil servant in the ministry of judiciary department in Mostar, in the Croatian community Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, will you tell us, how would you describe the relationship between you, as the presiding judge of the district military court in Travnik, and Mr. Aleksovski as the warden of the district military prison? How would you describe that relationship?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was largely official. Sorry, it was at a higher level. It was -- he was a professional, that is a person who worked in such penitentiary institutions even before the war, so if I could establish the contact very quickly, and I am not speaking only for myself, but also for other judges, and I can say that it was a highly professional contact, at least as far as my competence, my jurisdiction went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, in those official contacts with Mr. Aleksovski, did you ever have -- were you superior to him? Did you ever issue some orders to Mr. Aleksovski regarding the treatment of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only as regards the criminal proceedings. That is, only within my powers as accorded to me by the Criminal Proceedings Act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, I will show you three documents, and I should like to ask you currently to tell us what kind of official correspondence is it, and what was its purpose. And, Your Honours, this is an order for the transfer of a detainee from the Kaonik facility to the penitentiary in Zenica. Mr. Registrar, if I can suggest that these documents be marked with a unique number, and then be given letters A, B and C.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Very well. This shall be documents D21/A, B, C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you deem it necessary that the documents be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, you can see a document here on the ELMO. Could you please comment upon it. I am not going to ask you about the criminal proceedings conducted against the accused in this case, nor do I want you to comment on the proceedings itself. All I am interested in is the procedure that was applied in case of this particular individual. Could you give a comment about that. You have before you an order requiring the district military detention unit, prison in Busovaca, that is the warden, Zlatko Aleksovski, to transfer this individual to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was issued on the 5th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Percinlic, that at the time it was possible to communicate between Kaonik and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, communication was possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did such situation last all the time? I am referring to the possibility of communicating, or was that an exceptional situation?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was possible to communicate. Communications were very good with the army court of the BiH, which we had full co-operation. And you can see that from this particular document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the district military court in Travnik, acting upon the request of the military court of the BiH Army, does that mean that that court carried out the transfer of the accused?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: We did that on the basis of the applicable provisions. Edin Zahirovic was under the competence of the district military court which had its seat in Zenica. Therefore, he was transferred to that particular court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us in brief what kind of procedure it was? You would issue an order for transfer and then what would follow?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: We would send the case to the competent court and then to the prosecutor in Zenica. We would usually do it in the morning hours. And then after, in the afternoon, an order would be issued which was usually faxed to the detention unit. And then, before the end of the day, the order would be acted upon by the prison authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness document 21/B. I think this is 25/C. We should have the document that precedes this one. What kind of document is this, Mr. Percinlic?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This is a typical document. It's a note on transfer that is compiled by the warden of the prison. This is something that is done upon each transfer, that is including the transfer of this particular person to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the document on the basis of which transfer was conducted, transfer of the detainee, from the Kaonik facility to the prison in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown document 21/C, please. What kind of document is this, Mr. Percinlic?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This document is the certification of the take over of the detainee in Zenica. It was issued on the same day, on the 5th of March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. These documents can be removed from the ELMO. We no longer need them. Mr. Percinlic, we have seen three documents that relate to one and the same case, is it true that this procedure of transfer of detainees was a common procedure at the time and did it function well?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a common procedure at the time as you can see from the date on the document, it functioned properly. It all took place within one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would tender these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you in agreement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, you've told us that you were the president of the district military court, but that at the same time you actually worked as a judge, you were a trial judge as well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a brief description of the procedure that was applied at the time in case a criminal offence was committed? Which were the bodies that were relevant in these proceedings, and what was the pretrial procedure in that case at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The procedure was the following: The perpetrators were the members of the military. When we learned about a criminal offence, it was the military police of the Croatian Defence Council that was involved at first. They would conduct all necessary investigative actions and after that a Prosecutor would become involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you, after a crime was committed, the military police was informed about that and it was then the responsibility of the military police to establish relevant facts in connection with that particular criminal offence, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the military police established relevant facts, then they would file a criminal report, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which judicial body was that criminal report submitted?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: To the district military Prosecutor with the seat in Travnik if we have the same area in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, so the military police would submit the criminal report to the district military prosecutor in Travnik, which cooperated with the district military court in Travnik, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would the military district Prosecutor do when they received a criminal report from the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: After appropriate action was taken upon the criminal report, if all the information was gathered, then the criminal report would go to the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor would submit the request to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which court?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: To the competent court. In this case it was the district military court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore the district military court was in charge of the investigation as well, in addition to the trial, was that the system that was applied?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Percinlic, in the first half of 1993, were there many cases that were acted upon by the district military court in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: There was a number of cases because there were many soldiers in that area at the time. There were not many civilians there and the perpetrators of criminal offences were mostly members of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, do you remember the structure, the nature of the criminal offences that were before your court?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: These offences related to common criminal cases, cases of assaults, physical assaults, and assaults on property. They represented 90 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any serious criminal offences here? I mean murders, rapes and so on.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: There were such cases as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, do you remember a case involving a murder of two members of the Muslim nationality which was investigated before your court? I am referring to two individuals that were killed in early 1993, in February, '93.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember there was only one case like that. I don't know the names of the individuals involved, all I know is that they were both Muslims. I don't remember the exact date, but I believe it may have been the end of January, maybe beginning of February, 1993. On that occasion I was called by Mr. Aleksovski and this was only the second or the third time that we spoke on the telephone and he described to me what the situation was and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, let me make it clear. Mr. Aleksovski called you on the telephone on one particular occasion, do you remember what was the reason of his call?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to remember the details, but I know that he informed me that two Muslims had been murdered. I don't remember the exact location, but I know that it was on the territory of the Busovaca Municipality. He told me that he had already informed the military police and that all necessary measures had been taken by the military police. That he had informed the military Prosecutor as well, who had issued orders to the military police for the actions that were necessary for the Prosecution to complete the case. He wanted to know my opinion and I told him that he had done everything in accordance with the applicable provisions, the provisions of the law on criminal procedure. And that we should try to perhaps speed it up with the military police and intervene so that the case can be completed as soon as possible. And this is what I did, I immediately called them, called the military police of the 7th battalion, I believe it was the 4th battalion. And they informed me on that occasion that all necessary steps had been already done, exterior examination of the body, the onsite investigation was already conducted and they told me that they would submit the criminal report through the usual system of communication and I believe this is what happened. The criminal report was submitted on the next day in the morning, I don't know at what time and the suspects were questioned on the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, I will now show you certain documents and I would kindly ask you to have a look at them and to explain to the court what they are and in which stage of the procedure they were submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: This will be document D-22/A and D-22/B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, you have a document in front of you which has been marked Document 22/A, could you explain to the court what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal report submitted by the 4th battalion of the military police in Vitez and the date is 11th February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This criminal report as we can see was submitted was against three individuals?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These three individuals were suspect in three criminal cases, can you tell us what criminal offences we have here?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal offence that is described in Article 36 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a serious crime, which was introduced into the Criminal Code in prior to the outbreak of the war. It's a special type of murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that, why do you say it's a special type of murder?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It is a special type of murder because it was believed that such murders were committed out of a national ethnic hatred, this is why it had such a significance for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a crime which is thought to be a more serious crime than the usual crime, let's call it, usual crime of murder?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a more serious crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, is that the case that you described to us when you talked about Mr. Aleksovski calling you on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you told us that after Mr. Aleksovski had informed the military police about the murders, the military police conducted certain measures which resulted in the submission of the criminal report to the competent military Prosecutor, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can this document be removed from the ELMO by the usher, please, and can the witness be given the next document in order, 22/B. The Defence would like to apologise for a poor copy of this document, but this is all we could get. The translation of the document is far more legible and I think that the translation is more useful for the court. Mr. Percinlic, this is the request to open proceedings, which were submitted by the district Prosecutor in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that this request was submitted in respect of four persons, whereas the criminal report was submitted in respect of three individuals, can you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This was done by the military police. One cannot, therefore, expect to have a highly qualified individuals working at the military police in view of the circumstances. However, the military prosecutor who is a very experienced professional, who has 19 years of experience as a civilian prosecutor and who was appointed military prosecutor later on, we can perhaps conclude that on the basis of the criminal report, he believed that four individuals were actually suspect for this specific crime. This is not the first time that this happened. We had cases like that. We had, for example, cases when police would submit a criminal report against two individuals and then four would end up being suspects. The problems here involve the problems of identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of procedure was applied thereafter in accordance with the law on criminal procedure that was applicable on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time? What followed the submission for request to open investigation proceedings? What is the role of the court after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Once it receives such a request, the court opens the file and then proceeds with the questioning of the suspects. These four individuals were detained in detention, so they were questioned right away. I don't have the case file, but after that, an order for detention is usually issued in view of the gravity of the crime. After that, the court will hear evidence, the evidence that is proposed by the Prosecutor in the request to open investigation. It's difficult to read, but this is what it states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So together with this document, the request to open proceedings, the Prosecutor would always submit a number of documents which would support his request, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, could you please turn to page 2 of this document? Could you have a look at the first paragraph on page 2, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I only have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence would like to clarify this misunderstanding. Does it mean that there is no page 2 in the Croatian original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, indeed, it is true that the page I have here, but I believe, perhaps we could take a break now and you can resolve the issue in the meantime. Is that all right with you Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, let us take a twenty minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I benefited from the break and I photocopied the second page of this document, which somehow disappeared from the documentation, but it was translated. And I asked the registrar to have it distributed so that I think we can now ask the witness to answer some questions relative to this second page. So will you please be so kind to -- I should like the techs to zoom this page so that we can see the whole page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have a request for investigation, which was submitted by the competent district military Prosecutor in Travnik. This is a common form of the request for investigation; is that correct? The witness nodded. So we have here the list of suspects; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the description of the crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this list also includes information about documents and facts on which the Prosecutor based his request that is reached constituting grounds for the request. Mr. Percinlic, will you look at the first passage of this request on the second page. Have you had a look at it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please comment on it? What is it about? What does the Prosecutor -- what is the Prosecutor requesting?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, he says which are those reasonable grounds to suspect that these four committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if these reasonable grounds, derived from the criminal report of the military police, then the statements of the suspects, the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the findings of the superficial examination of the bodies, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, it means that all that the actions required by the Criminal Proceedings Act requested were performed and that the -- and that an expert, rather a physician performed that -- the requested activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether such an examination was performed?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In view of the circumstances, I was not in Busovaca when all that happened, but the practice applied in other municipalities also was to do it either in health centres or morgues, that is special premises in the immediate vicinity of health centres. You need to know that there were very many similar cases during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And does it emerge, then, from this document that the Prosecutor received also a document with the findings of the superficial examination of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, will you please look at item 2 on the second page of the request where the Prosecutor proposes the evidence that a Prosecutor should tender. Could you explain, perhaps, to us why does the judge propose to the Prosecutor to call in the relatives of the murdered and ask them about their claim?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, that meant to call in them and to ask them what would be the amount of the claim and whether they were interested or not to have the criminal proceedings conducted to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that kind of -- is that kind of request or is that kind of proposal a usual procedure in such cases in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is in cases like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please have a look at item 4 of the Prosecutor's proposal suggesting that forensic expert be called in to give his opinion on the basis of the findings of the -- after the superficial examination of the bodies. Is that also common procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is also a common procedure, because the superficial examination of bodies was usually done by a general practitioner, and this particular case they also wanted the expert finding of a forensic expert who would then give his final opinion, his final judgment about all the injuries, the cause of injuries, and all other relevant circumstances. So on the basis of which the forensic expert would base his view, on the basis of the findings on the superficial examination of the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the usher please remove the documents from the ELMO, because we shall not need them any more. Mr. Percinlic, you said that the roads were not safe, that the situation was precarious because of the armed conflicts and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally have such experience? I mean your personal security.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time, but I did later in June and July, '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We are not interested in that. Thank you. Mr. Percinlic, you said that after the communication was re-established you came to Kaonik for supervision, I think you said it was sometime in mid-March '93 or -- well, I think it was the latter half of March. And you said that it was the first time that you met Mr. Aleksovski in person?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, perhaps, what clothes he had on?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to say what kind of clothes he wore on that day, but in that area it was common, and I know from my own experience too, that people wore, if I may say so, parts of the military uniform or a complete military uniform. Because those who had fled from their family house had no time to take along all that they needed, so that often times people wore different kinds of clothes, parts of military uniforms with civilian trousers, something else. And the prison would -- did the same. And my colleagues, who had escaped from some nearby municipality did likewise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the guards wore in the prison, in the Kaonik Prison?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The guards were by and large in uniform, almost all of them. They were military police members, so they were members of military units, and they had their appropriate uniforms with appropriate insignia. So they were military persons and, in principle, they had to wear their military uniform to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if Mr. Aleksovski was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of any other military formation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, can we go back for a moment to the district military court in Travnik and the court records. We saw here some documents indicating that before the competent court criminal proceedings were being taken against persons charged with the murder of two Bosniaks, Muslims. Do you -- what happened next? Do you know whether a court record was made?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was filed, and the court record was opened. That is the common practice. But towards the end of May, in the second half of June, armed conflicts broke out in the town of Travnik itself, and they took place right by the building, next to the building of the military court, where two military courts sat. That is a military court of the Army of BiH and the military court of the HVO. And the only objective we had in mind was to get the personnel and the judges out of the court. So a large number of the records, about 80 percent of all the records, stayed behind in Travnik and perished, I guess. I know nothing of the fate of these records. But the military prosecutor managed to rescue his documentation from the building, that is, to bring them to Vitez, and it was only '94 and 1995 that all the cases were reconstructed, that is renewed. So my guess would be that the same applies to this particular case, because all the records were preserved. Whereas the court records, a very large portion of them, were destroyed during those military operations. But I would not know how, whether they were burned or taken away. I do not know that, because that day the town fell, if I may say so, under the control of the BiH Army. And all the members of the HVO, civilian structures and HVO military part left the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have to leave Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your other colleagues, other judges?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Percinlic, these documents that I showed to you are part of the documentation that was preserved by the prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, know if this document -- if this record survived or not, or is it that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: All the prosecutor records survived. No, the court records have not been preserved. Only one -- I'm sorry, only some cases, some cases, that is those referring to petty offences survived, because, you know, the files were rather small or rather thin and they could be taken along. But those records, those files which were bulky, simply could not be carried away and that was that. And that is how they perished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I see. Do you know, perhaps, the fate of this particular case, or is it that you know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I do not know what its fate was, but I know that in 1994, in '95, all of these cases were reopened, that is the cases were reconstructed, but I left that post after that, so I do not know what happened with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Let us go back to Kaonik, Mr. Percinlic. Can I have the assistance of the usher, please, and can the witness be shown the photograph that's been admitted into evidence under P/50. It is not a particularly clear photograph, but I think it will serve our purpose. Mr. Percinlic, do you recognise the place in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the premises of the district military prison in Kaonik, Busovaca. And according to these characteristic triangles on the walls, it is those premises, and the general appearance would seem to indicate that, and this stove in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the background you see a table. Do you recognise that table?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a dining table

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We do not need the photograph any more. You can remove it from the ELMO. Thank you. Your Honours, the Defence will now show the witness a document which represents the leaflet of the International Red Cross. It is a promotional leaflet which was published by the International Red Cross. It was published in Zagreb and there are several photographs in it. I shall now ask the usher to show this promotional material to the witness. And my question to the witness will be if he can recognise one of those photographs included in the promotional material of the International Red Cross. I have already given the Prosecutor's office a copy of this material, and they have one copy. I suggest that one be included in the records, one for the witness, but I also have more photocopies and I shall give them now to Your Honours. So the view we have in mind is not to use the text of this material as evidence. It is only a photograph. If the witness can identify it we shall hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, will you go carefully through these photographs and tell us if you can identify the photograph, I mean the place where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only the photograph on page number 4. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One photograph. Will you please place the document on the ELMO, and will you then indicate with your finger which photograph you have in mind. Yes. Mr. Percinlic, what do you see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, these are evidently the premises of the district military prison in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What makes you think that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, the characteristic door with these triangles, which is not a characteristic of prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is small photograph, but can you recognise somebody in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only one individual. Only one individual. I guess that is him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, perhaps, point to that person?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but one can't see it well on the machine, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps use the pencil. Mr. Percinlic, who is that, do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It's Fuad Kaknjo from Vitez, who is now with me on the regional government in Travnik

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please remove this photograph from the ELMO and show the witness another photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D/23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, this is a much clearer photograph. Do you recognise someone here?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only Fuad Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate with your pencil -- yes. Mr. Percinlic, in view of the place, the individual, and the clothes he is wearing, was this photograph taken at the same place as the previous photograph? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
